title: Study Skills
description: Free Study Skills guide built on learning research: how memory works, retrieval practice and spacing, note-taking, time management, reading textbooks, test-taking, focus and habits. 80 practice questions with explanations, 48 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: How Memory Works

concepts.intro: Memory has three stages, and studying can fail at any of them.
b: Encoding: getting information into memory. Paying attention and thinking about meaning helps
Storage: keeping information over time; sleep helps consolidate new memories
Retrieval: getting information back out when you need it, which is what tests measure
Working memory holds only a few items at once, so cramming too much at a time overloads it
Long-term memory is effectively unlimited, but information must be connected to be found again

concepts.intro: Without review, we forget quickly, but each review slows forgetting.
b: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) found memory for new material drops steeply within the first day or two
Reviewing at spaced intervals flattens the curve, so knowledge lasts longer
Feeling like you 'know it' right after reading is often misleading: familiarity isn't the same as recall
Forgetting isn't failure: retrieving something you've partly forgotten strengthens memory more
Plan reviews before a test rather than one long session the night before

concepts.intro: Meaningful, connected information is easier to store and retrieve.
b: Elaboration: explain ideas in your own words and connect them to what you already know
Dual coding: combine words with visuals such as diagrams, timelines and sketches
Concrete examples make abstract ideas easier to remember
Mnemonics (acronyms, memory palaces) help for lists and sequences
Sleep: an all-nighter hurts both encoding the next day and consolidation of what you studied

keyFacts: Memory stages: encoding, storage, retrieval.
Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve: fast early forgetting, slowed by spaced review.
Working memory has very limited capacity.
Sleep consolidates learning.
traps: Familiarity from rereading feels like learning but often isn't recall.
All-nighters trade sleep, which memory depends on, for extra study time.
Mnemonics help with lists but don't replace understanding concepts.

units.name: Active Recall & Spaced Repetition

concepts.intro: Testing yourself is one of the most effective ways to learn, not just to measure learning.
b: The testing effect: practicing recall produces better long-term retention than restudying (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006)
Methods: flashcards, practice problems, blank-page recall, answering end-of-chapter questions without looking
Always check answers afterward: feedback corrects errors
A 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing as a high-utility technique
Low-stakes quizzes work; you don't need a grade for the effect

concepts.intro: Spreading study over time beats massing it into one session.
b: The spacing effect: the same total study time produces better long-term memory when spread out
Cramming can work for tomorrow's test but is forgotten quickly
Expanding intervals: review after a day, then a few days, then a week
Flashcard systems (Leitner boxes, spaced-repetition apps) automate the schedule
Distributed practice was also rated high-utility in the Dunlosky review

concepts.intro: Mixing problem types trains you to choose the right method.
b: Blocked practice does many problems of one type in a row; interleaved practice mixes types
Interleaving feels harder but improves the ability to pick the right strategy on a test
It works especially well in math and science where problem types look similar
Combine with spacing: revisit old topics mixed in with new ones
'Desirable difficulties' feel harder during practice but improve long-term learning

keyFacts: Testing effect: recall practice beats rereading.
Spacing effect: spread out study time for long-term retention.
Interleaving: mixing problem types builds strategy choice.
Dunlosky et al. (2013): practice testing and distributed practice rated high utility.
traps: Cramming isn't useless for tomorrow, but it fails for the final exam and beyond.
Interleaving feels less productive during practice. That's normal.
Flashcards only help if you try to recall the answer before flipping.

units.name: Note-Taking Systems

concepts.intro: Good notes help encoding during class and give you material for retrieval practice later.
b: Notes should capture main ideas, examples and connections, not every word
Writing in your own words forces processing, which improves encoding
Studies comparing laptop and handwritten notes suggest verbatim transcription is less effective than summarizing (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014), though later replications found smaller effects
Review notes within 24 hours to fill gaps while memory is fresh
Notes are raw material: turn them into questions to test yourself

concepts.intro: A page layout built for review and self-testing.
b: Divide the page: a narrow cue column on the left, a wide notes column on the right, a summary area at the bottom
During class, take notes in the right column
After class, write questions or keywords in the cue column
Cover the notes and answer the cue questions from memory
Write a 2–3 sentence summary at the bottom of each page

concepts.intro: Match the format to the material.
b: Outline method: hierarchical headings and subpoints; good for well-organized lectures
Mind maps: a central idea with branches; good for seeing connections
Charting/table method: columns for comparing items (e.g. causes, effects and dates of wars)
Sketchnotes combine drawings and words (dual coding)
Use abbreviations and symbols consistently to keep up with lectures

keyFacts: Summarize in your own words instead of transcribing.
Cornell layout: cue column, notes column, summary.
Review notes within 24 hours.
Turn notes into questions for retrieval practice.
traps: Copying slides word for word feels productive but involves little thinking.
Beautiful notes aren't the goal. Notes you test yourself from are.
Don't rely on one format for everything; comparisons fit charts better.

units.name: Time Management

concepts.intro: Seeing all your commitments in one place prevents last-minute crunches.
b: Use one planner or calendar for classes, tests, work, activities and deadlines
Break big projects into small tasks with their own due dates
Plan backward from due dates: what needs to be done by when?
Estimate time realistically: most people underestimate (the planning fallacy)
Schedule study blocks like appointments rather than hoping to find time

concepts.intro: Not every task deserves the same attention.
b: Eisenhower matrix: sort tasks by urgent/not urgent and important/not important
Do important and urgent tasks first; schedule important but not urgent ones before they become crises
The 'most important task' approach: pick 1–3 key tasks each day
Say no or delay low-importance commitments when overloaded
Review your plan weekly and adjust

concepts.intro: Procrastination is usually about avoiding an unpleasant feeling, not laziness.
b: Make starting easy: commit to just five minutes
Break vague tasks ('study bio') into concrete actions ('answer 10 practice questions on cell transport')
The Pomodoro Technique: 25 minutes of focused work, then a 5-minute break
Implementation intentions: 'If it is 4 p.m., then I will start my history outline'
Reward progress and track streaks to build momentum

keyFacts: Break big projects into dated small tasks.
Planning fallacy: people underestimate how long tasks take.
Eisenhower matrix: urgent vs. important.
Pomodoro: 25 minutes of work, 5-minute break.
traps: Being busy isn't the same as being productive. Check that tasks are important.
A to-do list with vague items ('study') is easy to avoid.
Multitasking usually slows you down and increases errors.

units.name: Reading Textbooks Efficiently

concepts.intro: A quick preview gives you a map, so details have somewhere to go.
b: Survey the chapter: title, headings, bold terms, graphics, summary and review questions
Turn headings into questions ('What causes inflation?')
Activate prior knowledge: what do you already know about this topic?
Decide your purpose: an overview, specific answers, or deep understanding
SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review

concepts.intro: Active reading means thinking, not just moving your eyes.
b: Read one section at a time, then look away and recite the main idea
Annotate sparingly: short margin notes in your own words beat heavy highlighting
Study figures and tables; they often carry key ideas
Monitor understanding: if a paragraph made no sense, reread or look up a term
Highlighting everything is a low-utility strategy on its own (Dunlosky et al., 2013)

concepts.intro: Consolidate before moving on.
b: Answer the questions you wrote from the headings without looking
Summarize the chapter in a few sentences or a concept map
Make flashcards for key terms and processes
Connect the chapter to class notes and earlier chapters
Schedule a spaced review of the chapter

keyFacts: SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
Preview headings and bold terms before reading.
Recite after each section to check understanding.
Heavy highlighting alone is low utility.
traps: Reading every word once doesn't mean you learned it.
Highlighting feels active but often isn't. Pair it with recall.
Skipping graphs and tables skips important content.

units.name: Test-Taking Strategies

concepts.intro: Test performance starts days before the test.
b: Find out the format (multiple choice, short answer, essay) and practice in that format
Take full practice tests under timed conditions
Review mistakes and understand why each wrong answer was wrong
Sleep the night before; retrieval is worse when you're sleep-deprived
Pack materials the night before to reduce morning stress

concepts.intro: Manage time and work strategically.
b: Skim the whole test first and budget time by point value
Answer easier questions first, marking hard ones to return to
Multiple choice: predict the answer before looking at choices, then eliminate wrong options
Watch for qualifiers like 'always', 'never', 'except' and 'not'
Essays: make a quick outline, state a clear thesis, and support it with specific evidence

concepts.intro: Some nervousness is normal, and there are proven ways to manage it.
b: Slow breathing (longer exhale than inhale) calms the body's stress response
Expressive writing about worries for 10 minutes before a test improved scores for anxious students in one study (Ramirez & Beilock, 2011)
Reframe arousal as excitement ('I'm ready') rather than fear
After a test, do an error analysis: content gap, careless mistake or misread question?
Changing an answer after careful reconsideration is more often right than wrong, despite the myth

keyFacts: Practice in the same format as the test.
Budget time by point value.
Eliminate wrong choices; watch for 'not' and 'except'.
Error analysis: content gap, careless error or misreading.
traps: 'Always stick with your first answer' is a myth; reconsidered changes more often help than hurt.
Don't spend 10 minutes on a 1-point question.
Rereading notes the morning of the test is weaker than a quick self-quiz.

units.name: Focus & Distraction Management

concepts.intro: Your brain can't truly focus on two demanding tasks at once.
b: 'Multitasking' is really rapid task-switching, which costs time and accuracy
After an interruption it can take a while to fully refocus
Notifications pull attention even when you don't respond
Studies have found that having a phone visible can reduce available attention, though effect sizes vary
Deep, uninterrupted focus produces more learning per hour than distracted study

concepts.intro: It's easier to change your surroundings than rely on willpower.
b: Put your phone in another room or use app blockers during study blocks
Close unneeded browser tabs and turn off notifications
Keep a consistent study spot associated with work
Have materials ready before you start to avoid 'quick' trips that turn into breaks
Instrumental music may help some people; lyrics tend to compete with reading

concepts.intro: Focus depends on your body as much as your intentions.
b: Schedule hard tasks when you're most alert
Take real breaks: move, stretch or get outside instead of scrolling
Regular sleep and exercise improve attention and mood
Stay hydrated and eat regular meals
Mindfulness practice can strengthen your ability to notice and redirect wandering attention

keyFacts: Multitasking = task-switching, which costs time and accuracy.
Remove temptations instead of relying on willpower.
Notifications interrupt attention even when ignored.
Breaks work best away from screens.
traps: Feeling good at multitasking doesn't mean you are.
Scrolling isn't a restful break. It often extends into lost time.
Willpower alone fails; design the environment.

units.name: Goal Setting & Habits

concepts.intro: Clear goals direct effort and make progress visible.
b: SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
'Raise my chemistry grade from 78% to 85% by the end of the quarter' beats 'do better in chemistry'
Process goals (study 30 minutes daily) are under your control; outcome goals (get an A) aren't fully
Break long-term goals into weekly targets
Track progress so you can adjust early

concepts.intro: Habits make good study behavior automatic, so it doesn't depend on motivation.
b: Habit loop: cue → routine → reward
Habit stacking: attach a new habit to an existing one ('after dinner, I review flashcards')
Start small so the habit is easy to repeat
Research suggests habits take weeks to months to become automatic, and it varies by person and behavior
Missing one day doesn't break a habit; getting back on track quickly matters most

concepts.intro: How you interpret setbacks affects what you do next.
b: Growth mindset (Dweck): believing abilities can improve with effort and strategy
Effective effort means changing strategies, not just working longer
Self-efficacy (Bandura): belief you can succeed, built through small wins
Intrinsic motivation (interest, mastery) tends to last longer than rewards alone
Reflect regularly: what worked, what didn't, what will I change?

keyFacts: SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Habit loop: cue, routine, reward.
Process goals are within your control.
Growth mindset: abilities develop with effort and strategy.
traps: 'Just try harder' isn't a growth mindset. Change strategies.
The '21 days to form a habit' figure isn't supported by research; it varies widely.
Outcome goals alone can feel discouraging; pair them with process goals.

quiz.q: Which stage of memory does a test directly measure?
o: Encoding
Storage
Retrieval
Sensory memory
quiz.e: A test asks you to pull information back out of memory.

quiz.q: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows that:
o: Memory fades only after several weeks have passed, whatever you do
Most forgetting happens soon after learning unless we review
Forgetting happens at a steady rate across the whole time
Reviewing right away has no effect on retention at all
quiz.e: The steepest drop comes early.

quiz.q: Why can rereading notes give a false sense of mastery?
o: Rereading is the strongest way to learn, so confidence matches mastery
It forces you to practice retrieving the material from memory every time
Notes usually contain wrong facts that you then have to unlearn later
Familiarity feels like knowing, but it isn't the same as recalling
quiz.e: Recognizing material is easier than producing it from memory.

quiz.q: Explaining a new idea in your own words and linking it to prior knowledge is called:
o: Cramming
Massed practice
Rote rehearsal
Elaboration
quiz.e: Elaboration builds meaningful connections.

quiz.q: Combining a written explanation with a labeled diagram is an example of:
o: Dual coding
Interleaving
Chunking
Rereading
quiz.e: Words plus visuals create two routes to the memory.

quiz.q: What does sleep do for learning?
o: Erases short-term memory permanently
Has no effect
Helps consolidate new memories
Only helps physical skills
quiz.e: Memories are stabilized during sleep.

quiz.q: Working memory is best described as:
o: A large, permanent store of everything you have learned
A system that records exact sounds for later playback
A storage area that holds facts for years at a time
A small, temporary workspace for current thinking
quiz.e: It holds only a few items at once.

quiz.q: ROY G. BIV for the colors of the rainbow is an example of:
o: A mnemonic
Dual coding
Spaced practice
Elaboration
quiz.e: An acronym mnemonic.

quiz.q: Which study plan fights the forgetting curve best?
o: Short reviews spread over several days
One long session the night before
Reading the chapter once carefully
Highlighting everything
quiz.e: Spaced reviews interrupt forgetting repeatedly.

quiz.q: Struggling to recall something you partly forgot, then succeeding, usually:
o: Weakens the memory because the effort is wasted
Strengthens the memory more than easy review
Makes no difference compared with simple rereading
Shows that you should stop studying that topic now
quiz.e: Effortful retrieval is a 'desirable difficulty'.

quiz.q: The testing effect means:
o: Taking tests only measures what you already knew before
Restudying beats practicing recall for long-term memory
Students perform better when they study less before tests
Practicing recall improves long-term memory more than restudying
quiz.e: Retrieval itself strengthens memory.

quiz.q: Which technique did Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate as high utility?
o: Highlighting
Rereading
Practice testing
Summarizing only
quiz.e: Practice testing and distributed practice received the highest ratings.

quiz.q: A student has 4 hours to study. Which plan is best for a test next week?
o: One 4-hour session the night before
Four 1-hour sessions on different days
Two hours of highlighting and two of rereading
Four hours the morning of the test
quiz.e: Spacing the same total time boosts retention.

quiz.q: Doing 20 problems mixing area, volume and perimeter instead of 20 area problems in a row is:
o: Blocking
Massed practice
Elaborative rehearsal
Interleaving
quiz.e: Mixing problem types is interleaving.

quiz.q: Why does interleaving help on tests?
o: It trains you to identify which strategy a problem needs
It lets you master one skill before touching the next
It makes practice feel easier and more fluent each time
It saves time by repeating the same problem type
quiz.e: Test problems appear mixed, not in labeled blocks.

quiz.q: The best way to use flashcards is to:
o: Try to recall the answer before flipping, then check
Read the answer first, then flip back to the question
Shuffle the cards only after the answer is memorized
Review each card only once to prevent boredom
quiz.e: The effort of recall is what builds memory.

quiz.q: A 'blank page' review means:
o: Leaving a page empty and rereading your notes silently, hoping to recall more
Writing everything you remember about a topic without notes, then checking
Copying the textbook onto fresh paper so the page is neatly filled
Highlighting every key idea on a clean page before you begin to study
quiz.e: It's free recall followed by feedback.

quiz.q: In a Leitner box system, cards you get wrong are:
o: Removed permanently
Reviewed more often
Reviewed less often
Studied only on test day
quiz.e: Missed cards move back to frequently reviewed boxes.

quiz.q: 'Desirable difficulties' are:
o: Obstacles that slow learning and should be avoided where possible
Study strategies that feel harder but improve long-term learning
Hard tasks that are simply too advanced for the student's level
Study methods that feel easy and so improve long-term learning
quiz.e: Spacing, interleaving and retrieval all feel effortful.

quiz.q: Why is feedback important during retrieval practice?
o: It corrects errors so you don't strengthen wrong answers
It shows you the length of time you have spent on it
It makes recalling the material feel easier next time
It replaces the need to recall the material again
quiz.e: Without checking, mistakes can be practiced into memory.

quiz.q: In the Cornell method, the left-hand cue column is used for:
o: Questions or keywords that prompt recall
Writing the full lecture word for word
Drawing diagrams for each of the main ideas
The date, class period and lecturer's name
quiz.e: Cues let you quiz yourself by covering the notes.

quiz.q: Why is summarizing in your own words better than transcribing?
o: It is faster because you write fewer words overall
It makes your notes look neater and more organized
It forces you to process and understand the material
It guarantees every detail is recorded exactly right
quiz.e: Processing meaning improves encoding.

quiz.q: Which note format is best for comparing the causes, dates and outcomes of three wars?
o: A single paragraph
A mind map with one branch
A verbatim transcript
A chart or table
quiz.e: Columns make comparisons easy.

quiz.q: A mind map is most useful for:
o: Recording long lectures in strict word-for-word order
Showing connections between ideas around a central topic
Listing facts in a single column, one idea at a time
Memorizing definitions through endless repetition
quiz.e: Branches show relationships visually.

quiz.q: When should you first review your notes?
o: Within about 24 hours
The night before the exam
Only if you missed class
Never
quiz.e: Early review catches gaps and slows forgetting.

quiz.q: The bottom section of a Cornell page is for:
o: Homework assignments
Vocabulary lists only
A short summary of the page
Doodles
quiz.e: Summarizing forces you to identify main ideas.

quiz.q: How can notes be used for retrieval practice?
o: Reread them several times before closing the book
Highlight all the key terms in a new color
Cover them and answer questions from memory
Copy them neatly into a fresh notebook again
quiz.e: Self-testing from notes uses the testing effect.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of weak notes?
o: Long verbatim sentences with no structure
Short phrases with clear headings and key terms
Questions in the margin to check later on
A summary written at the end of each page
quiz.e: Transcription without structure is hard to review.

quiz.q: The outline method works best when:
o: The lecture jumps between topics without any order
You need to draw links between ideas across many topics
The speaker gives mostly examples with no clear structure
The lecture is clearly organized into topics and subtopics
quiz.e: Outlines mirror hierarchical structure.

quiz.q: Sketchnotes combine words and drawings, which applies:
o: Massed practice
Blocked practice
Dual coding
Rote copying
quiz.e: Words and images create two memory routes.

quiz.q: The planning fallacy is the tendency to:
o: Overestimate how long tasks will take
Finish tasks early after you start working
Underestimate how long tasks will take
Break big tasks into steps and plan them
quiz.e: People expect tasks to go faster than they do.

quiz.q: In the Eisenhower matrix, studying for an exam two weeks away is:
o: Important but not urgent
Urgent but not important
Neither
Urgent and important
quiz.e: It matters but has no immediate deadline, so schedule it now.

quiz.q: The Pomodoro Technique uses:
o: Long study sessions of two hours with no breaks at all in between
Focused work intervals (often 25 minutes) followed by short breaks
Random breaks that depend entirely on your mood in the moment
Quick twenty-minute naps taken before and after each session
quiz.e: Short sprints help sustain focus.

quiz.q: Which to-do item is most likely to get done?
o: Answer 10 practice questions on chapter 4
Do better in math class by trying harder
Study chapter 4 sometime this week as you can
Get ready for the unit test with more studying
quiz.e: Concrete, specific actions are easier to start.

quiz.q: Planning backward from a due date means:
o: Doing the easiest task first and delaying all the harder ones
Waiting until the due date comes before planning any steps
Setting deadlines for each step working back from the final due date
Starting the final step first, then skipping the rest of it
quiz.e: It spreads the work so nothing piles up.

quiz.q: Procrastination is best understood as:
o: Avoiding the uncomfortable feeling a task causes
A sign of laziness and poor character in a student
A problem caused by a lack of time to finish tasks
A shortage of information about how to do the task
quiz.e: Research frames it as emotion regulation.

quiz.q: 'If it's 7 p.m. after dinner, then I'll review flashcards' is an example of:
o: An implementation intention
The planning fallacy
Multitasking
Blocked practice
quiz.e: If–then plans make starting automatic.

quiz.q: Why is multitasking usually counterproductive?
o: Switching between tasks costs time and increases errors
Doing several tasks at once saves a large amount of time
The brain handles two demanding tasks in parallel with ease
It improves accuracy because you are using more attention
quiz.e: Task-switching has a cognitive cost.

quiz.q: A weekly review of your plan helps you:
o: Avoid changing your plan so you stay on one track
Adjust priorities and catch upcoming deadlines
Finish all your tasks for the week ahead of time
Memorize everything you studied during the week
quiz.e: Regular check-ins keep the plan realistic.

quiz.q: The 'just five minutes' strategy works because:
o: You are guaranteed to work for several hours afterward
Starting is often the hardest part, and momentum follows
Five minutes is all the study time that you really need
The task becomes easier because it was too hard before
quiz.e: Once started, people often continue.

quiz.q: The 'S' in SQ3R stands for:
o: Summarize
Skim only
Study
Survey
quiz.e: Survey the chapter first.

quiz.q: Turning a heading into a question before reading helps because:
o: It makes the chapter shorter so you read faster
It lets you skip the paragraphs below the heading
It gives you a purpose and something to answer
It replaces the need to read the details in the text
quiz.e: Reading to answer a question is active.

quiz.q: Which is the most effective active-reading habit?
o: Highlighting as many sentences as you can on each page you read
Rereading each paragraph twice before you go on to the next one
Pausing after each section to recite the main idea without looking
Copying key sentences into your notes word for word as you go
quiz.e: Recitation is retrieval practice.

quiz.q: Why study a chapter's figures and tables?
o: They are decoration with no useful information
They often summarize key relationships and data
They repeat the text word for word with no new content
They are only used by teachers to fill empty space
quiz.e: Visuals frequently hold core content.

quiz.q: According to Dunlosky et al. (2013), highlighting on its own is:
o: A low-utility strategy
The most effective strategy
Equal to practice testing
Harmful in all cases
quiz.e: It rarely improves learning by itself.

quiz.q: Activating prior knowledge means:
o: Memorizing the headings so you can repeat them after
Reading the summary before you start the first chapter
Skipping the parts you already know on the page
Thinking about what you already know before reading
quiz.e: Connections make new information easier to store.

quiz.q: After finishing a chapter, the best next step is to:
o: Answer your heading questions from memory and make flashcards
Move on to the next chapter right away without looking back
Reread the chapter from the start until it feels familiar
Highlight the entire chapter in several different colors
quiz.e: Consolidate with retrieval before moving on.

quiz.q: Monitoring comprehension means:
o: Reading faster when the material gets hard to follow
Noticing when you don't understand and fixing it
Counting how many pages you have finished in an hour
Checking that your notes are neat and fully copied
quiz.e: Catch confusion before it piles up.

quiz.q: Short margin notes in your own words are better than heavy highlighting because they:
o: Require you to process the meaning
Look neater
Take no time
Cover more of the page
quiz.e: Writing in your own words is elaboration.

quiz.q: When previewing a chapter, which should you look at?
o: Only the first paragraph and the first page
Only the practice questions at the chapter end
Every word of every sentence, from start to finish
Headings, bold terms, graphics and the summary
quiz.e: A survey builds a mental map.

quiz.q: What is the best first step when you receive a test?
o: Begin at question one and go in order
Start with the hardest question first
Spend half your time on the first part
Skim the whole test and plan your time
quiz.e: A quick scan lets you budget time by points.

quiz.q: On multiple choice, a good strategy is to:
o: Read all the choices first, then pick the longest one that sounds right
Choose the first answer that seems familiar and move on at once
Change your answers often, since your first instinct is usually wrong
Predict the answer before reading choices, then eliminate wrong ones
quiz.e: Predicting avoids being swayed by tempting distractors.

quiz.q: Research on changing answers suggests that:
o: Changes after careful reconsideration are more often correct than not
Changing is helpful only when you were guessing at random at first
Most changes turn right answers into wrong ones, so never change
First instincts are always correct, so changes should be avoided
quiz.e: Studies consistently find more wrong-to-right changes than right-to-wrong.

quiz.q: An essay answer should start with:
o: A long restatement of the prompt
A list of unrelated facts
An apology for running out of time
A clear thesis that answers the question
quiz.e: A thesis guides your evidence.

quiz.q: A question asks which choice is NOT a cause of the war. Your first step is to:
o: Notice the word NOT and look for the exception
Pick the choice that looks most like a cause
Skip it, since negative wording is a trick
Choose the longest option, which is usually right
quiz.e: Qualifiers change what the question asks.

quiz.q: Which strategy can reduce test anxiety right before a test?
o: Studying all night to cover the topics you may have missed
Skipping breakfast so that you feel sharper in the room
Slow breathing or brief expressive writing about worries
Telling yourself that you will fail to lower expectations
quiz.e: Both have research support.

quiz.q: An error analysis after a test helps you:
o: Decide which teacher grades more harshly than the other teachers do
Identify whether mistakes came from content gaps, carelessness or misreading
Show that you should simply study longer for every future test you take
Prove that the test was unfair and that the questions were misleading
quiz.e: Different causes need different fixes.

quiz.q: The best preparation for a timed essay test is to:
o: Write practice essays under timed conditions
Read your notes slowly so facts feel familiar
Memorize a model essay and write it out
Outline answers mentally without writing
quiz.e: Practice in the real format and time limit.

quiz.q: How should you handle a hard question you can't answer quickly?
o: Stay on it until you solve it, however long
Guess at once and never look at it again
Leave it blank and skip similar questions
Mark it, move on, and return if time allows
quiz.e: Protect time for questions you can answer.

quiz.q: Why is sleep the night before important?
o: Sleep removes everything you studied from your memory
Staying awake makes your attention and recall sharper
You can make up lost sleep during the actual test
Sleep deprivation impairs attention and retrieval
quiz.e: A rested brain retrieves better.

quiz.q: What actually happens when you 'multitask' on two demanding tasks?
o: You process both tasks fully at the same time, with no loss
You do both faster because your brain works in parallel
You switch rapidly between them, losing time and accuracy
Your accuracy improves as each task keeps you alert
quiz.e: Task-switching has a real cost.

quiz.q: The most effective way to handle phone distractions while studying is to:
o: Put the phone out of sight or in another room
Keep it face up on your desk, sound off
Keep it beside your book and check hourly
Leave alerts on and resist them by willpower
quiz.e: Removing the cue is easier than resisting it.

quiz.q: Which is the best kind of study break?
o: Opening social media
A short walk or stretch
Starting a TV episode
Playing a long video game
quiz.e: Screen breaks tend to run long and don't rest attention.

quiz.q: Why can music with lyrics hurt reading comprehension?
o: Lyrics are quieter than instrumental music, so you focus less
Singing along improves reading speed and keeps you alert
Music with lyrics has no effect on any kind of reading task
Lyrics compete with the language processing reading needs
quiz.e: Both use verbal processing.

quiz.q: Studying in the same focused spot helps because:
o: The room becomes quiet only when you stay in one spot
Your brain stores the facts in the walls of that room
The place becomes associated with concentration
Moving around always makes you forget what you studied
quiz.e: Cues in the environment trigger habits.

quiz.q: When should you do your hardest study task?
o: When you're most tired
When you're usually most alert
Right before bed only
During class
quiz.e: Match task difficulty to energy.

quiz.q: Turning off notifications helps focus because:
o: Each alert interrupts attention even if you ignore it
You will no longer know what time it is while you study
Alerts only distract you when you actually open the message
Your phone battery lasts longer, which helps you study more
quiz.e: Interruptions carry a refocusing cost.

quiz.q: Mindfulness practice can help studying by:
o: Improving your ability to notice and redirect wandering attention
Removing every thought from your mind while you are reading
Making you read faster so that you finish the work early
Replacing sleep, since meditation gives the same rest at night
quiz.e: It trains attention control.

quiz.q: Having all materials ready before you begin helps because:
o: It guarantees you will remember all you read
It makes you feel more rushed and so you work faster
It means you never need any breaks during a session
It prevents small trips that become long breaks
quiz.e: Fewer interruptions, more focus.

quiz.q: Regular exercise affects studying by:
o: Making you tired so you study less
Replacing the need to study for tests
Improving attention, mood and sleep
Having no effect on mood, focus or rest
quiz.e: Physical activity supports cognitive function.

quiz.q: Which is a SMART goal?
o: Do better in math this semester by working a lot harder on each unit
Complete 20 practice problems every weeknight until the test on May 10
Study hard every day and try to earn an A on every test this year
Finish as many problems as possible before the next test arrives soon
quiz.e: It is specific, measurable and time-bound.

quiz.q: A process goal is:
o: A result you hope for, such as earning an A in the class
A grade target that depends on how your teacher marks
A behavior you control, like studying 30 minutes a day
A wish about your final rank among your classmates
quiz.e: Process goals focus on actions.

quiz.q: The habit loop consists of:
o: Goal, plan, test
Survey, question, read
Cue, routine, reward
Encode, store, retrieve
quiz.e: A cue triggers a routine that is reinforced by a reward.

quiz.q: 'After I brush my teeth, I'll review five flashcards' is an example of:
o: Blocked practice
Habit stacking
The planning fallacy
Interleaving
quiz.e: It attaches a new habit to an existing one.

quiz.q: How long do habits take to form, according to research?
o: Exactly 21 days for everyone and every habit
Only one week, whatever the habit is
More than a year for all habits in all cases
It varies widely, often weeks to months
quiz.e: Studies find large differences by person and behavior.

quiz.q: A student with a growth mindset who fails a test is most likely to:
o: Blame the teacher and avoid studying for the next test
Look at what went wrong and change study strategies
Decide they are simply not smart enough for the class
Study the same way, but hope for luck the next time
quiz.e: Growth mindset treats setbacks as feedback.

quiz.q: Self-efficacy is:
o: The ability to remember exactly what you read
How much more you know than your peers
Belief in your ability to succeed at a task
A feeling of anxiety that you feel before a test
quiz.e: Bandura's concept, built through experiences of success.

quiz.q: Which motivation tends to last longest?
o: External rewards such as money for grades
Pressure from parents to hit a set result
Fear of punishment if grades are too low
Intrinsic interest in mastering the subject
quiz.e: Intrinsic motivation is more durable.

quiz.q: If you miss a day of a new study habit, the best response is to:
o: Get back on track the next day
Give up; the habit is broken
Double the work forever
Start over in a month
quiz.e: Consistency over time matters more than perfection.

quiz.q: Why start a new habit small?
o: Small actions are easier to repeat until they become automatic
Big changes work better than small ones from the first day
Small habits give faster results than large ones ever could
Starting small avoids any need to plan for the future
quiz.e: Early repetition builds automaticity.

quiz.q: Which type of memory holds information for only a few seconds unless you rehearse it?
o: Procedural memory
Semantic memory
Long-term memory
Short-term (working) memory
quiz.e: Working memory is limited in both time and capacity.

quiz.q: Chunking helps memory by:
o: Grouping items into meaningful units
Making each item longer and more detailed
Storing single letters one at a time
Repeating each item until it sounds alike
quiz.e: A phone number is easier to hold as three groups than ten digits.

quiz.q: Sleep after studying helps because it:
o: Makes reading faster
Replaces practice
Consolidates new memories
Erases old notes
quiz.e: Memory consolidation happens during sleep.

quiz.q: Mnemonics work best when they:
o: Are long, complex and as abstract as they can be made
Repeat the same fact until it can be recited at once
Link new information to something vivid or familiar
Replace the need to understand the actual material
quiz.e: Vivid associations make recall easier.

quiz.q: Active recall means:
o: Rereading your notes until they feel very familiar now
Highlighting the main ideas as you read through them
Copying the answers from your book onto flashcards
Trying to retrieve information without looking at it
quiz.e: Retrieval practice strengthens memory more than rereading.

quiz.q: Spaced repetition schedules reviews:
o: At increasing intervals
All in one night
Only before the exam
Randomly with no pattern
quiz.e: Reviewing just before you would forget makes memories last.

quiz.q: Cramming the night before is usually:
o: Just as effective as study spread across several days
More effective for long-term memory than spaced study
Less effective for long-term retention than spaced study
The best method when the test is more than a month off
quiz.e: Cramming helps short-term recall but fades quickly.

quiz.q: Which is an example of active recall?
o: Using flashcards and answering before flipping
Rereading a chapter and highlighting each key term
Copying definitions neatly into a new notebook page
Watching a video of the lesson a second time over
quiz.e: Answering first forces retrieval.

quiz.q: Interleaving practice means:
o: Studying one single problem type until mastered
Repeating the same problem many times in a row
Studying a topic only on the day it is taught
Mixing different problem types in one session
quiz.e: Mixing topics improves your ability to choose the right method.

quiz.q: The Cornell note-taking system divides the page into:
o: Notes, cues and a summary
Lists of vocabulary
Three equal columns of definitions
Pictures only
quiz.e: Cornell notes include a cue column and a summary section.

quiz.q: Notes are most useful when you:
o: Review and rewrite them soon after class
Wait until just before the test to read them
Never look at them again after class ends
Copy them word for word from a classmate
quiz.e: Reviewing within a day reduces forgetting.

quiz.q: An outline format is best for:
o: Ideas that have no clear order or hierarchy at all
Material with clear main ideas and subpoints
Showing links between ideas that cross over topics
Drawing pictures around one central image
quiz.e: Outlines show hierarchy.

quiz.q: A concept map is helpful for:
o: Listing the facts in lecture order
Recording every word the teacher says
Memorizing a single bare definition
Showing relationships between ideas
quiz.e: Maps connect concepts with links.

quiz.q: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks by:
o: Cost and size
Difficulty and age
Urgency and importance
Length and color
quiz.e: It helps you decide what to do first and what to drop.

quiz.q: Breaking a big project into smaller steps helps because it:
o: Adds more work
Removes deadlines
Makes the work less overwhelming
Guarantees perfection
quiz.e: Small tasks are easier to start and track.

quiz.q: The planning fallacy is:
o: Overestimating how long tasks will take
Underestimating how long tasks will take
Believing planning ahead wastes your time
Finishing projects well before deadlines
quiz.e: Add buffer time to your estimates.

quiz.q: Procrastination is often reduced by:
o: Waiting until you feel motivated first
Setting a large goal for the whole task
Starting with a very small first step
Telling yourself to just try much harder
quiz.e: Starting builds momentum.

quiz.q: The SQ3R method begins with:
o: Review
Recite
Survey
Read aloud only
quiz.e: SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.

quiz.q: Before reading a chapter, it helps to:
o: Preview headings and summaries
Memorize every word
Skip the first page
Read the index only
quiz.e: Previewing builds a mental framework.

quiz.q: Turning headings into questions helps because it:
o: Gives your reading a purpose
Makes the text longer
Replaces reading
Hides main ideas
quiz.e: Questions focus attention on answers.

quiz.q: Summarizing a section in your own words:
o: Is only for English
Checks and deepens understanding
Replaces testing
Wastes time
quiz.e: If you can't summarize it, you may not understand it yet.

quiz.q: On a multiple-choice test, a good first step is to:
o: Answer easy questions first and return to hard ones
Start with the hardest questions while you are fresh
Answer every question in order and never skip any
Guess on every question before you read through them
quiz.e: This secures easy points and manages time.

quiz.q: Process of elimination is useful because it:
o: Lets you skip questions that look hard
Raises your chance of guessing correctly
Guarantees you will get the right answer
Saves time since you skip reading choices
quiz.e: Removing wrong options improves the odds.

quiz.q: Before writing an essay answer, you should:
o: Write the longest possible answer
Start without thinking
Skip the question
Plan a quick outline
quiz.e: A short plan keeps the answer organized.

quiz.q: Test anxiety can be reduced by:
o: Studying all night to feel fully ready
Avoiding all practice before the test
Practicing under test-like conditions
Telling yourself the test doesn't matter
quiz.e: Familiarity lowers stress.

quiz.q: Multitasking while studying usually:
o: Improves memory
Reduces learning quality
Doubles learning
Has no effect
quiz.e: Switching tasks costs attention.

quiz.q: A good way to limit phone distraction while studying is to:
o: Check it every five minutes
Place it on your desk face up
Keep notifications on
Put it in another room
quiz.e: Out of sight lowers the temptation.

quiz.q: Working in a consistent place helps because it:
o: Builds a cue for focus
Increases noise
Eliminates breaks
Makes tests easier
quiz.e: Context cues can trigger a study mindset.

quiz.q: SMART goals are:
o: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound
Simple, Memorable, Accurate, Rewarding and Time-limited
Strong, Motivating, Attainable, Realistic and Timely
Specific, Measurable, Active, Rigid and Test-oriented
quiz.e: SMART goals are clear and trackable.

quiz.q: Habit stacking means:
o: Keeping all your habits in one big pile of tasks
Dropping an old habit to make room for a new one
Doing a new habit at a random time during each day
Attaching a new habit to an existing routine
quiz.e: For example, review flashcards right after brushing your teeth.

quiz.q: A growth mindset is the belief that:
o: Failure is permanent
Practice is useless
Abilities can improve with effort
Talent is fixed
quiz.e: Carol Dweck's research links this belief with persistence.

quiz.q: How long can working memory hold information without rehearsal?
o: Several hours, and a large number of separate items
About ten minutes, and as many as twenty items
Days at a time, when the information is repeated
Only seconds to under a minute, and just a few items
quiz.e: Working memory is limited, so rehearsal and chunking help move information into long-term memory.

quiz.q: Which approach most effectively builds long-term memory?
o: Repeating facts out loud until they sound familiar
Connecting new ideas to what you already know
Rereading the chapter again just before the test
Highlighting each line in several bright colors
quiz.e: Elaboration creates links that make recall easier.

quiz.q: Retrieval practice means:
o: Rereading your notes until they seem familiar
Highlighting the main ideas in a bright color
Copying the textbook word for word on a page
Testing yourself from memory instead of rereading
quiz.e: Pulling information out strengthens memory more than passive review does.

quiz.q: Which habit best fights the 'illusion of knowing'?
o: Rereading the chapter again and again before a test
Closing the book and explaining the idea from memory
Highlighting each line in several different colors
Listening to a recording of the lecture while resting
quiz.e: Feeling familiar with material is not the same as being able to recall it.

quiz.q: Which note-taking format best shows relationships among ideas?
o: A concept map
A word-for-word transcript
A list of dates
A single paragraph
quiz.e: Maps use links and branching to show how ideas connect.

quiz.q: Why should you review notes soon after class?
o: Forgetting is fastest right after learning
Notes are easier to read when they are older
Memory holds steady whenever you delay it
Your teacher can check how neat your notes are
quiz.e: A quick review slows the forgetting curve.

quiz.q: 'Eating the frog' means:
o: Saving the hardest task until the end of the day
Doing the easiest and quickest tasks before any others
Skipping any task you do not feel like starting now
Doing your hardest or most important task first
quiz.e: Tackling the hardest task early prevents procrastination.

quiz.q: Underestimating how long a task will take is known as:
o: Spaced repetition
The planning fallacy
Chunking
Interleaving
quiz.e: Adding a time buffer to estimates helps schedules stay realistic.

quiz.q: SQ3R stands for:
o: Skim, Quiz, Rewrite, Repeat, Revise
Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review
Study, Query, Reread, Rest, Reflect
Scan, Quote, Reread, Record, Rank
quiz.e: It is a structured method for reading textbooks actively.

quiz.q: Before reading a chapter in detail, you should:
o: Read the first sentence of each paragraph only
Memorize the key terms from the glossary first
Survey headings, summaries and review questions
Skip straight to the first paragraph and read it
quiz.e: A preview gives you a framework for new information.

quiz.q: Active reading includes:
o: Reading faster without stopping
Reading only the first sentence of paragraphs
Listening to music at high volume
Annotating and asking questions as you read
quiz.e: Engaging with the text improves understanding and retention.

quiz.q: If there is no penalty for guessing and you are unsure, you should:
o: Leave the answer blank
Always pick the first choice
Eliminate wrong choices and guess
Change answers randomly
quiz.e: Eliminating options improves your odds.

quiz.q: Which strategy can reduce test anxiety?
o: Staying up all night to study
Practice tests and slow, controlled breathing
Avoiding all review
Comparing your answers with classmates during the test
quiz.e: Familiarity with the format and calming techniques lowers stress.

quiz.q: Keeping your phone out of sight while studying helps because:
o: It helps you hear alerts from far away
Its mere presence can pull attention away
It makes study time pass more slowly
It is a way for it to run low on battery sooner
quiz.e: Removing cues reduces the urge to check the device.

quiz.q: A SMART goal is:
o: Short, Memorable, Attractive, Realistic and Timely
Simple, Meaningful, Active, Rewarding and Tough
Set, Measured, Adjusted, Recorded and Tested
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound
quiz.e: A goal such as 'finish two practice quizzes by Friday' follows this model.

quiz.q: An 'if-then' plan (implementation intention) helps habits by:
o: Linking a specific cue to a planned action
Making you decide at random each time what to do
Replacing any cue with a general wish to improve
Relying on motivation to start a task each day
quiz.e: For example: 'If it's 4 p.m., then I start homework.'

quiz.q: The 'forgetting curve' shows that:
o: Memory fades quickly without review
Memory stays stable for years on end
Forgetting only happens when you sleep
Old memories fade before new ones
quiz.e: Spaced review slows forgetting.

quiz.q: Which sleep behavior helps memory?
o: Sleeping enough after learning
Skipping sleep before tests
Napping never
Studying all night
quiz.e: Sleep helps consolidate memories.

quiz.q: The testing effect is the finding that:
o: Rereading the material improves later memory more than testing
Practicing retrieval improves later memory more than restudying
Taking a test only measures learning and never changes it
Highlighting a text creates stronger memories than recall
quiz.e: Self-testing strengthens memory.

quiz.q: The Leitner flashcard system works by:
o: Putting all of the cards in one daily pile
Reviewing the cards you know most often
Moving cards you know to less frequent review
Sorting the cards alphabetically each day
quiz.e: Hard cards appear more often.

quiz.q: Which makes flashcards more effective?
o: Writing a question on one side and an answer on the other
Copying a whole textbook paragraph onto each side of a card
Putting the question and the answer together on one side
Making each card a long summary of an entire chapter section
quiz.e: Short prompts invite retrieval.

quiz.q: Highlighting is most effective when:
o: You highlight sparingly and then review
You mark every line, then never reread
You use many colors on each single page
You mark whole paragraphs to skip text
quiz.e: Selective marking forces decisions.

quiz.q: The outline method of note-taking:
o: Organizes ideas in a hierarchy
Uses only drawings
Records every word
Avoids headings
quiz.e: It shows relationships between main points and details.

quiz.q: A good strategy for notes from a video is to:
o: Keep playing and copy every spoken word
Watch it once at double speed, no notes
Pause and write key ideas in your own words
Wait until it ends, then try to recall it
quiz.e: Paraphrasing aids understanding.

quiz.q: A realistic study schedule should include:
o: No breaks
Only weekends
Eight hours straight
Breaks and buffer time
quiz.e: Buffers absorb surprises.

quiz.q: The best time to study a hard subject is usually:
o: Late at night
When you have the most energy
Right before bed always
Never
quiz.e: Match difficult tasks to peak focus.

quiz.q: Previewing a chapter's headings helps because:
o: It lets you skip the text of the chapter
It shows which questions are on the exam
It replaces taking notes while reading
It builds a mental outline before you read
quiz.e: A framework helps comprehension.

quiz.q: When a passage is confusing, you should:
o: Speed up so the meaning comes later
Skip it and hope it is not tested
Highlight it all and then move right on
Slow down and reread, then summarize
quiz.e: Monitor your comprehension.

quiz.q: Annotating a text means:
o: Writing questions and comments in the margins
Copying the whole text onto a fresh page
Underlining every sentence in one color
Reading aloud to a friend, with no notes
quiz.e: It makes reading active.

quiz.q: Before an exam, you should:
o: Study all night
Skip breakfast
Avoid review
Get a good night's sleep
quiz.e: Sleep helps recall.

quiz.q: When reviewing a test, the most useful step is to:
o: Analyze why you missed each question
Check your score, then file the test
Compare your grade with classmates
Memorize the answers on the paper
quiz.e: Understanding errors prevents repeats.

quiz.q: On a timed test, you should:
o: Spend all time on question one
Ignore the clock
Skip the instructions
Budget time for each section
quiz.e: Pacing prevents running out of time.

quiz.q: The 'two-minute rule' says that if a task takes less than two minutes, you should:
o: Postpone it
Ignore it
Do it right away
Delegate it
quiz.e: Small tasks add clutter if delayed.

quiz.q: Single-tasking is better than multitasking for studying because:
o: Fast task switching speeds up the brain
Switching tasks reduces focus and efficiency
Doing two things doubles what you learn
Mixing tasks keeps you more alert for longer
quiz.e: Attention is limited.

quiz.q: A good study environment is:
o: Loud, busy and close to a television
Quiet, organized and free of distractions
Comfortable, dim and next to your bed
Crowded, social and full of friends
quiz.e: Cues in the environment shape behavior.

quiz.q: Rewarding yourself after finishing a task can:
o: Make it harder
Have no effect
Reduce motivation
Reinforce the habit
quiz.e: Rewards strengthen repeated behavior.

quiz.q: An accountability partner helps because:
o: Someone completes your work for you
Someone stores your notes until exams
Someone else learns the material for you
Someone expects you to follow through
quiz.e: Social commitment boosts consistency.

quiz.q: Which is an example of spaced practice?
o: Studying vocabulary for 15 minutes on five different days
Studying vocabulary for 75 minutes on the night before a test
Studying vocabulary for an hour on one single weekend day
Studying vocabulary for five minutes right before the class
quiz.e: Spacing sessions improves retention.

quiz.q: A good question to ask while reading is:
o: What page does this section end on?
How fast can I finish the chapter?
Which words here are in bold type?
What is the main idea of this section?
quiz.e: Questions focus attention on meaning.

quiz.q: Which helps you return to focus after a distraction?
o: Writing down the distraction and getting back to the task
Scrolling on your phone for a bit to calm yourself down
Starting a different task so the first one can wait longer
Telling yourself the day is lost and stopping for good
quiz.e: A capture list keeps stray thoughts from derailing you.

flashcards.d: Getting information into memory, helped by attention and meaning.

Sort tasks by urgent/important to decide what to do first.

Setting step deadlines working back from a final due date.
Delaying a task to avoid negative feelings about it.
Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
Scanning headings, bold terms, visuals and summary before reading.
Stating the main idea from memory after a section.
Noticing and fixing confusion while reading.
Brief margin notes in your own words.
Diagram linking ideas from a chapter.
Allocate minutes by point value after skimming the test.
Cross out wrong choices to raise your odds.
Words like always, never, not and except that change a question's meaning.

Classifying mistakes: content gap, careless or misread.
Writing about test worries beforehand, which can reduce anxiety's effect.
Time and accuracy lost when switching between tasks.
Arranging surroundings to remove distractions.
Extended, uninterrupted focus on a demanding task.
Movement or rest away from screens.
Scheduling hard tasks at peak alertness; sleep, exercise, food.

PART_A.q: A student reads a chapter once and feels confident, but can't answer questions the next day. The most likely reason is:
o: Familiarity was mistaken for recall
They studied too much
Their working memory is full
Sleep erased it
PART_A.e: Recognition feels like knowing but isn't retrieval.

PART_A.q: Which schedule best uses the spacing effect for a test on Friday?
o: Short sessions Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday
One long session Thursday night
Two sessions Friday morning
One session the previous Friday only

PART_A.q: Which note-taking method is designed for self-testing?
o: Verbatim transcription
Highlighting the textbook
Recording the lecture
Cornell notes
PART_A.e: The cue column turns notes into questions.

PART_A.q: A student says 'I'll work on the project this week' and never starts. The best fix is to:
o: Wait for motivation
Work on it only the night before
Break it into specific tasks with deadlines
Remove it from the calendar
PART_A.e: Concrete, dated steps are easier to act on.

PART_A.q: The 'Recite' step of SQ3R is an example of:
o: Massed practice
Dual coding
Highlighting
Retrieval practice
PART_A.e: Stating ideas from memory is retrieval.

PART_A.q: During a test, a student spends 15 minutes on a 2-point question. They should have:
o: Spent even longer
Skipped the rest of the test
Marked it and returned after easier questions
Changed all answers

PART_A.q: Which study environment is best for focus?
o: In bed with TV on
A quiet spot with the phone in another room
At a desk with notifications on
A crowded cafeteria with a phone out

PART_A.q: 'I'll study better' becomes a SMART goal when changed to:
o: 'I'll study a lot'
'I'll try my best'
'I'll do 15 minutes of flashcards each weeknight until my Spanish test on the 20th'
'I'll get smarter'

PART_B1.q: Which pair of techniques combines two memory strategies?
o: Rereading twice
Highlighting in two colors
Drawing a labeled diagram while explaining it aloud
Copying notes twice
PART_B1.e: It uses dual coding and elaboration.

PART_B1.q: Mixing old and new problem types in each practice session combines:
o: Blocking and cramming
Highlighting and rereading
Interleaving and spacing
Transcribing and outlining
PART_B1.e: Revisiting old topics mixed with new ones does both.

PART_B1.q: A student's notes are pages of full sentences copied from slides. The best advice is:
o: Summarize in your own words and add questions to test yourself
Write even faster
Use more colors
Stop taking notes
PART_B1.e: Processing and self-testing make notes useful.

PART_B1.q: Which item belongs in the 'important but not urgent' quadrant?
o: Answering a ringing phone
A deadline in one hour
Starting a research paper due in three weeks
Scrolling social media
PART_B1.e: Scheduling it now prevents a crisis later.

PART_B1.q: Before reading, turning 'The Causes of the French Revolution' into 'What caused the French Revolution?' is the:
o: Review step
Recite step
Question step of SQ3R
Survey step

PART_B1.q: A student lost points because they missed the word 'EXCEPT' in several questions. Their error analysis category is:
o: Content gap
Misreading the question
Time management only
Test anxiety only
PART_B1.e: The knowledge was there; the question was misread.

PART_B1.q: Why is a 5-minute break walking outside better than 5 minutes on social media?
o: Walking burns more calories
Social media is banned
It restores attention without pulling you into more distraction
They're equally good
PART_B1.e: Screen breaks often extend and fragment attention.

PART_B1.q: Tracking a daily study streak mainly supports:

Habit formation through visible progress and reward
Blocked practice

PART_B2.q: Explain why testing yourself is more effective than rereading, and describe two ways to do it.
PART_B2.sa: Retrieval practice strengthens memory by making you reconstruct information, and it reveals what you don't know, whereas rereading builds familiarity that feels like learning but often isn't recall. Two methods: flashcards where you answer before flipping, practice problems or questions without notes, blank-page recall of a topic, or covering Cornell notes and answering the cue questions. Check answers afterward for feedback.

PART_B2.q: Describe a realistic weekly plan for a student with a test Friday, a project due next Wednesday and sports practice daily.
PART_B2.sa: A strong answer puts fixed commitments (school, practice) on a calendar first, then schedules short spaced study sessions for the test Monday through Thursday, and breaks the project into dated steps (research, outline, draft, revise) spread across the week and weekend. It builds in buffer time for the planning fallacy, includes sleep, and uses specific tasks rather than vague 'study' blocks.

PART_C.q: A friend says, 'I'm just not a math person. I study for hours and still fail.' Using at least three strategies from this course, write advice that could help them.
PART_C.sa: A strong response addresses mindset and method. It reframes ability with a growth mindset (skills improve with effective strategies, not just hours). It replaces passive study (rereading notes, watching examples) with retrieval practice (working problems without looking at solutions) and interleaving problem types. It spaces sessions across the week instead of cramming, and does error analysis after quizzes to target gaps. It also sets SMART process goals (e.g. 10 mixed practice problems nightly) and manages focus by removing phone distractions.

PART_C.q: Explain how memory's three stages (encoding, storage, retrieval) connect to three specific study strategies.
PART_C.sa: Encoding: elaboration or dual coding makes information meaningful and connected, so it's stored well. Storage: spaced review and sleep consolidate memories and slow the forgetting curve. Retrieval: practice testing strengthens the pathways used to recall information and shows what needs more work. The strongest answers explain why each strategy works for its stage.

workedExamples.title: Spacing a review
workedExamples.prompt: You have a test in 14 days. Sketch a spaced review plan for one chapter.
steps: First review right after learning
Then review on days 2, 5 and 10
Finish with a practice test two days before
workedExamples.answer: Review on day 1, then days 2, 5 and 10, with a practice test around day 12

workedExamples.title: Plan a project
workedExamples.prompt: A 10-page paper is due in 10 days. How should you break it up?
steps: Break it into stages
Research, outline, draft, revise and proofread
Give yourself about one day for each stage plus buffer
workedExamples.answer: About 1 page per day with research, outline, draft, revision and proofreading scheduled

workedExamples.title: Chunking a list
steps: Working memory holds a limited number of items, so group them.
Split the list into pairs: 91, 47, 25, 83.
Say the chunks aloud and rehearse them.

workedExamples.title: Cornell notes
workedExamples.prompt: How do you set up a page for Cornell notes?
steps: Draw a narrow left column for cues and questions.
Use the wide right column for notes during the lecture.
Leave a box at the bottom for a short summary written after class.
workedExamples.answer: Three sections: cues, notes and summary.

workedExamples.title: Planning a study week
workedExamples.prompt: You have three tests next week. How do you plan?
steps: List each test date and how long you need for each subject.
Schedule short sessions across several days rather than one long night.
Put review of the earliest test first and leave a buffer day.
workedExamples.answer: Spread sessions over the week and review earlier material again.

workedExamples.title: Using SQ3R
workedExamples.prompt: How do you use SQ3R on a textbook chapter?
steps: Survey headings and summaries, then turn each heading into a question.
Read to answer each question and recite the answer in your own words.
Review all the questions at the end.

workedExamples.title: Process of elimination
workedExamples.prompt: You are unsure which of four choices is correct. What do you do?
steps: Cross out choices you know are wrong.
Compare the remaining ones against the question's key words.
Choose the best remaining answer and move on.
workedExamples.answer: Eliminating wrong choices raises your chance of picking the right one.

workedExamples.title: Setting a SMART goal
workedExamples.prompt: Turn 'get better grades' into a SMART goal.
steps: Make it specific: choose one class.
Make it measurable and time-bound: pick a target and a date.
Make it achievable and relevant to your plans.
workedExamples.answer: Raise my math grade from a B to an A by completing every homework assignment this month.
